title: A Closed Form Depth-Width Law for Neural Collapse in Deep Linear Networks

paper.title: A Closed Form Depth-Width Law for Neural Collapse in Deep Linear Networks
paper.abstract:
Abstract How depth and width of neural networks shape learned representations is usually studied only after
training. We show that, in a tractable feature-learning setting, this
dependence can instead be obtained in closed form. Using neural collapse as a
probe of representation geometry, we express NC1–NC3 directly in terms of the
learned feature kernel, extending an identity known for NC1 to the angular part
of NC2 and to NC3 under a ridge readout. For deep linear networks with
exchangeable class structure, the resulting kernel equations yield a geometric
law, exact within the theory, for the layerwise evolution of within-class
variability.
At large width, the accumulated compression becomes a function of the depth-to-width ratio L / N L/N , with its rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior and architecture. Numerical experiments support the derived
dependence on depth, width and signal-to-noise ratio. The result is a
representation-level scaling law derived from feature-learning theory rather
than fitted after training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Allocating a fixed budget between depth and width changes what a network learns, but the effect is usually measured after training rather than derived in advance. Proportional depth–width analyses have previously identified the depth-to-width ratio as a controlling parameter for finite-width kernel fluctuations, kernel renormalization, and effective depth ( Hanin and Nica, 2020 ; Li and Sompolinsky, 2021 ; Hanin and Zlokapa, 2023 ) ; here we show that the same architectural ratio controls a representation-level observable. Neural collapse (NC) describes the progressive emergence of low within-class variability, simplex-like class means, and classifier–mean alignment ( Papyan et al., 2020 ) . Empirical work has observed increasingly separated or collapsed representations across depth ( He and Su, 2023 ; Rangamani et al., 2023 ) , raising the question of what governs this evolution and how it depends on data and architecture. Existing theory has studied unconstrained-feature optima ( Hong and Ling, 2024 ) , perturbations of this idealization ( Tirer et al., 2023 ) , intermediate-layer compression under structural assumptions on trained weights ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and data-dependent kernel descriptions ( Kothapalli and Tirer, 2025 ) . Here we instead extend the kernel formulation of NC1 Kothapalli and Tirer (2025) to NC2 and NC3, and evaluate the resulting observables on the self-consistent feature-learning kernels of Fischer et al. (2024) . Under exchangeable class geometry, the resulting deep-linear equations reduce to scalar within- and between-class channels, yielding the following contributions: • Kernel forms for NC2 and NC3, extending the NC1 identity of Kothapalli and Tirer (2025) , so that all three training-set observables are computable from the feature kernel and the labels. • An exact geometric law for layerwise representation compression in exchangeable deep linear networks, showing that the accumulated compression is controlled at leading order by the depth-to-width ratio, with the collapse rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior, and architecture.

sections.heading: Beyond the solvable regime.
sections.text: The kernel identities of Theorem 1 are not restricted to linear or exchangeable networks. We therefore ask whether they remain informative when the exact depth law no longer applies. Figure 2: NC1, NC2 and NC3 on four-class XOR ( N = 256 N=256 , L = 3 L=3 ), computed from the self-consistent kernel theory and from trained finite-width networks. Error bars denote variation across seeds. On nonlinear four-class XOR, Figure 2 shows that NC1, NC2 and NC3 evolve in the same direction across depth in the self-consistent kernel solution and in trained finite-width networks. Agreement is strongest in the earlier layers, while trained networks typically reach stronger terminal collapse. We therefore interpret this experiment not as a validation of the exact L / N L/N law outside the linear exchangeable setting, but as evidence that the kernel observables continue to capture the qualitative evolution of learned representation geometry. Implementation details, solver tolerances, SGLD hyperparameters, seed countsare given in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: We showed that NC1–NC3 can be evaluated directly from the feature kernel and class labels, without explicitly forming the feature coordinates. Combining these kernel observables with self-consistent feature-learning theory makes representation geometry predictable from the data, prior, and architecture without training each candidate network. For exchangeable deep linear networks, we further derived an exact geometric law for the layerwise evolution of NC1. At large width, the accumulated compression is controlled at leading order by L / N L/N , with its rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior, and architecture. This provides a tractable representation-level scaling law that links architectural choices directly to learned geometry. Extending such predictive laws to nonlinear networks and general data geometry remains an important direction.

sections.heading: Appendix A Derivation of the kernel neural-collapse observables [Theorem 1]
sections.text: We prove that the neural-collapse observables in Theorem 1 can be written entirely in terms of the feature kernel and the class labels. We work at an arbitrary fixed layer and make no assumption here on the network architecture, training dynamics, or exchangeability of the data. We consider C C balanced classes with n = P / C n=P/C samples per class and one-hot label matrix Y ∈ ℝ P × C Y\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times C} . Denote by μ c \mu_{c} the mean representation of class c c and by μ G \mu_{G} the global mean. We use the sample- and class-centering matrices H = I P − 1 P ​ 𝟏 P ​ 𝟏 P ⊤ , H C = I C − 1 C ​ 𝟏 C ​ 𝟏 C ⊤ , H=I_{P}-\frac{1}{P}\mathbf{1}_{P}\mathbf{1}_{P}^{\top},\qquad H_{C}=I_{C}-\frac{1}{C}\mathbf{1}_{C}\mathbf{1}_{C}^{\top}, and the centered label matrix Y c = H ​ Y . The proof consists of three independent steps, corresponding to the three observables in Theorem 1 . For NC1, we show that fixed label-dependent projectors separate the representation into its within-class residual and centered class-mean components; their squared norms are therefore traces of projected kernel matrices. For NC2, we show that the Gram matrix of the centered class means is obtained by applying the class-averaging and centering operators directly to K K . For NC3, we first derive the representer form of the bias-free ridge readout and then express its cosine alignment with the centered class means through kernel inner products. Together these three constructions show that NC1, angular NC2, and ridge-readout NC3 require no explicit coordinates for the representation once K K and the labels are known. The NC1 kernel identity was previously derived by Kothapalli and Tirer [2025] ; we reproduce it in our notation because the same sample-space decomposition is used later in the exchangeable linear analysis. The kernel forms of angular NC2 and ridge-readout NC3 are new.

We show that, in a tractable feature-learning setting, this dependence can instead be obtained in closed form. Using neural collapse as a probe of representation geometry, we express NC1–NC3 directly in terms of the learned feature kernel, extending an identity known for NC1 to the angular part of NC2 and to NC3 under a ridge readout. For deep linear networks with exchangeable class structure, the resulting kernel equations yield a geometric law, exact within the theory, for the layerwise evolution of within-class variability. At large width, the accumulated compression becomes a function of the depth-to-width ratio L / N L/N , with its rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior and architecture. Numerical experiments support the derived dependence on depth, width and signal-to-noise ratio. The result is a representation-level scaling law derived from feature-learning theory rather than fitted after training. * * footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction Allocating a fixed budget between depth and width changes what a network learns, but the effect is usually measured after training rather than derived in advance. Proportional depth–width analyses have previously identified the depth-to-width ratio as a controlling parameter for finite-width kernel fluctuations, kernel renormalization, and effective depth ( Hanin and Nica, 2020 ; Li and Sompolinsky, 2021 ; Hanin and Zlokapa, 2023 ) ; here we show that the same architectural ratio controls a representation-level observable. Neural collapse (NC) describes the progressive emergence of low within-class variability, simplex-like class means, and classifier–mean alignment ( Papyan et al., 2020 ) . Empirical work has observed increasingly separated or collapsed representations across depth ( He and Su, 2023 ; Rangamani et al., 2023 ) , raising the question of what governs this evolution and how it depends on data and architecture. Existing theory has studied unconstrained-feature optima ( Hong and Ling, 2024 ) , perturbations of this idealization ( Tirer et al., 2023 ) , intermediate-layer compression under structural assumptions on trained weights ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and data-dependent kernel descriptions ( Kothapalli and Tirer, 2025 ) . Figure 1 separates verification of the analytic solution from its comparison with trained networks. Panels (a)–(c) consider the exactly exchangeable population-kernel setting: the closed-form geometric law agrees with the numerical fixed-point solution across depth, reproduces the data-dependent contraction rate, and exhibits the predicted leading dependence on τ = L / N \tau=L/N under g ℓ = 1 g_{\ell}=1 . Panel (d) asks the distinct question of whether this behavior persists in a finite trained network. The SGLD-trained network shows approximately geometric layerwise decay over several orders of magnitude, despite deviations from the idealized population-kernel setting. Beyond the solvable regime. The kernel identities of Theorem 1 are not restricted to linear or exchangeable networks. We therefore ask whether they remain informative when the exact depth law no longer applies. Figure 2: NC1, NC2 and NC3 on four-class XOR ( N = 256 N=256 , L = 3 L=3 ), computed from the self-consistent kernel theory and from trained finite-width networks. Error bars denote variation across seeds. On nonlinear four-class XOR, Figure 2 shows that NC1, NC2 and NC3 evolve in the same direction across depth in the self-consistent kernel solution and in trained finite-width networks. Agreement is strongest in the earlier layers, while trained networks typically reach stronger terminal collapse. We therefore interpret this experiment not as a validation of the exact L / N L/N law outside the linear exchangeable setting, but as evidence that the kernel observables continue to capture the qualitative evolution of learned representation geometry. Implementation details, solver tolerances, SGLD hyperparameters, seed countsare given in Appendix E . 4 Conclusion We showed that NC1–NC3 can be evaluated directly from the feature kernel and class labels, without explicitly forming the feature coordinates. Combining these kernel observables with self-consistent feature-learning theory makes representation geometry predictable from the data, prior, and architecture without training each candidate network. For exchangeable deep linear networks, we further derived an exact geometric law for the layerwise evolution of NC1. At large width, the accumulated compression is controlled at leading order by L / N L/N , with its rate determined self-consistently by the data, prior, and architecture. This provides a tractable representation-level scaling law that links architectural choices directly to learned geometry. Extending such predictive laws to nonlinear networks and general data geometry remains an important direction.
